deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page (Litt. F) is a worked example of Gauss's method of orbit determination. It is applied to three Ceres observations of 1802, each 59 days apart: Jan 25 (Méchain, Paris), Mar 25 (Maskelyne, Greenwich) and May 23 (Piazzi, Palermo, on the next page). The total span is 118 days. The marginal note Dec 7 / 49 / 59 / 59 / 167 Tage adds a possible fourth observation of 1801 Dec 7: 49+59+59 = 167 days. Geocentric distances are taken from Gauss's 'VII. Elemente' of Ceres. This page reduces observations 1 and 2 to the quantities the method needs: Earth's heliocentric longitude V and log R, and for the planet the ecliptic coordinates (λ, β), the inclination η and the arc p. The next page combines these into spherical intersections P, P', P''.

A. TIME REDUCTION (obs. 1). Paris mean time 16h14m28.5s.
- Light-time correction: log Δ = 0.27776 (from the VII elements), plus 2.6875 = log 486.9 s (light time per AU), gives 2.96526, i.e. 923.1 s = 15m23.1s. This is subtracted.
- Paris→Seeberg longitude difference: +33m35.0s.
- Result: 16h32m40.4s = 16h.544555 = Jan 25.6893565 days (counted from Jan 0). log t = 1.40975.
- 9.13731 = log 0.13718″/day, i.e. general precession of about 50.1″/yr. Then t·0.13718 = 3.52″, the precession reducing to the mean equinox 1802.0.
- Obs. 2: log Δ 0.20755 + 2.6875 gives 785.3 s = 13m5.3s. Then 11h56m46s − 13m5.3s + 42m56.0s (Greenwich→Seeberg) = 12h26m36.7s = 12h.4435278, i.e. day 84.5184803 (Jan 31 + Feb 28 + 25 = 84). log = 1.92695, and precession 11.59″.

B. SOLAR (EARTH) PLACE from tables (von Zach type).
- Mean longitude: epoch 9s9°23′57.38″ + 24°38′28.25″ + 40′46.20″ = 304°43′11.83″.
- Equation of centre +50′6.53″ (read 56′ in the image; the sum requires 50′) and −0.16″, giving 305°33′18.20″.
- Perturbations −7.49, +7.42, +0.77 and +20.00″: the tables include aberration −20″, so the true place is wanted because light time has already been removed from the time. This gives 305°33′38.90″.
- Minus 3.52″ precession, plus 180°: V = 125°33′35.38″.
- Log-radius side: argument columns summed mod 1000 (745 420 944 19); R = 0.9848590 + 8 − 12 + 150 + 76 = 0.9848812, log R = 9.9933838.
- Obliquity: 23°27′55.57″ + 9.49″ nutation = 23°28′5.06″.
- Obs. 2: 279°23′57.38″ + 58°9′11.48″ + 24°38′28.25″ + 30′39.74″ = 2°42′16.85″. Then +1°54′54.53″ − 0.42″ = 4°37′10.96″. Then −7.46 − 2.14 − 1.47 + 20.00 gives 4°37′19.89″. Minus 11.59″ precession gives 4°37′8.30″.
- Obs. 2 radius: R = 0.9983141, log R = 9.9992672. Obliquity 23°28′4.90″.

C. PARALLAX (right margins). Only declination parallax is applied (meridian observations): Δδ = π☉ sin(φ − δ)/Δ, with π☉ = 8.6″ (log 0.93450).
- Paris, φ = 48°50′14″: 0.93450 + 9.72224 (= −log Δ) + log sin 36°53′48″ = 0.43516, i.e. 2.72″.
- Greenwich, φ = 51°28′39″: 2.96″.
- Palermo (next page): 1.63″.

D. EQUATORIAL → ECLIPTIC (classical auxiliary angle N).
- Obs. 1: α = 188°20′53.2″, δ = 11°56′29.12″, ε = 23°28′5.06″.
- tan N = tan δ / sin α gives N = −55°31′49.17″; N − ε = −78°59′54.23″.
- tan λ = tan α · cos(N − ε)/cos N, with log ratio 9.5278679, gives λ = 182°49′57.49″.
- tan β = tan(N − ε) sin λ gives β = 14°15′44.84″.
- Check: cos β = cos δ (sin α / sin λ) cos(N − ε)/cos N = 9.9864033.
- Obs. 2: α = 181°54′18.8″, δ = 17°43′52.76″, ε = 23°28′4.90″. N = −84°3′49.77″ and N − ε = −107°31′54.67″, giving λ = 174°27′56.99″ and β = 16°58′33.99″ (cos β 9.9806516).

E. GREAT CIRCLE THROUGH THE ANTI-SOLAR POINT (V, 0) AND THE PLANET (λ, β).
- Formulas: tan η = tan β / sin(λ − V); cos p = cos β cos(λ − V); sin p = sin β / sin η. Here η is the circle's inclination to the ecliptic and p the arc from the point of longitude V to the planet.
- Obs. 1: λ freed of nutation = 182°49′55.34″, minus V of date 125°33′38.90″, gives λ − V = 57°16′16.44″. Then η = 16°48′48.08″ and p = 58°23′57.04″ (sin and cos values agree).
- Obs. 2: nutation 3.04″ is instead added to the Sun, giving V' = 184°37′22.93″ and λ − V' = −10°9′25.94″. Then tan η negative, η' = 120°0′50.23″, and p' = 19°42′20.47″ (log sin 9.5278730, log cos 9.9737913).
- These η, p and V are the inputs to the next page's 'Combinationen'. There the intersections of these great circles are formed (P, P', P'', q, q''), as in Gauss's method published in the Summarische Übersicht (1809).
errors: Equation of centre transcribed '+56′6.53″' is inconsistent with the sum 305°33′18.20″, which requires +50′6.53″. 50′ is also the physically correct value for mean anomaly about 25°. This is either a misreading or a pure writing slip; the arithmetic downstream uses 50′.

No genuine computational errors found. All recomputed logarithms agree to about 1 unit in the 5th–6th decimal: tan δ, sin α, N, λ, β, cos β, η, p, the light times, parallaxes, precession and solar sums.

The struck value 125°33′38.90″ is actually the one used for λ − V on obs. 1. This is consistent: both λ (nutation removed) and V are referred to the mean equinox of date. The struck line is not an error.
Simplifications, not mistakes: the parallax ignores RA parallax and the Earth's flattening; the light-time constant 486.9 s corresponds to an aberration constant of exactly 20″.

results.what: Reduction of observation time for light-time (t − Δ·486.9 s) using a geocentric distance from provisional elements, and use of true (aberration-free) solar place
results.modern_name: Light-time correction / planetary aberration via time shift
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century practice; systematized by Gauss (Theoria Motus 1809, art. 118)

results.what: Equatorial to ecliptic conversion via auxiliary angle N (tan N = tan δ/sin α, tan λ = tan α cos(N−ε)/cos N, tan β = tan(N−ε) sin λ)
Diurnal parallax in declination Δδ = π sin(φ−δ)/Δ for meridian observations

For each observation, the great circle through the anti-solar point (V,0) and the geocentric planet place: inclination η and arc p; inputs for intersecting these circles in an orbit determination from three observations
results.modern_name: Gauss's geometric (great-circle) orbit determination method of 1801–1802, published in 'Summarische Übersicht' (1809)

results.what: Reduction of solar tables (mean longitude, equation of centre, perturbations, aberration, nutation, precession to mean equinox 1802.0)

deep.surprise_reason: A careful numerical worked example of Gauss's own, already published, orbit method applied to 1802 Ceres data. The method is known as his (Summarische Übersicht 1809, Theoria Motus); the page is an archival detail, not a new result.

checkable.asserts: sin p = sin β / sin η gives the same p1
aberration 20″ corresponds to light time ≈ 487 s ≈ 10**2.6875
solar longitude 305°33′18.20″ = 305.55506° requires equation of centre 50′6.53″, not 56′

transcription_corrections: Title: 'die 11[?] Tage' should read 'die 118 Tage' (59 + 59 days).
'+ 56. 6,53' (equation of centre, obs. 1) must be '+ 50. 6,53' for the sum 305°33′18.20″ to hold.
Obs. 2: '107.31.54,67' is N − ε = −107°31′54.67″; log sin α '8,5217429' carries the negative sign (n).
'Latit. a nutatione purgata' is attached to the longitude 182°49′55.34″ (longitude freed of nutation); the latitude is 14°15′44.84″.
Marginal 0.93450 = log 8.6″ (solar parallax); 48°50′14″, 51°28′39″, 38°6′45″ are the latitudes of Paris, Greenwich, Palermo.
